comments.text:
The problem with a central bank is when the instruction is "cut pensions and public sector salaries" and not "tax the billionaires." 

Pensioners can't afford pay cuts. They're living at the edge of poverty already. And public sector salaries aren't making anyone rich either, but having people with secure taxpayer-funded jobs can really stabilise a town's economy as those people reliably have enough money to buy groceries and get the car serviced. Breaking that reliability breaks everything downstream of it. 

Meanwhile if a billionaire has a few million less in the bank, nobody is going to suffer from that. We could charge them a 99% income tax, including on concealed income like when they borrow against shares, and they'd still be a whole lot richer than any honest person. But central banks never tell the government "you need to tax the billionaires." It's a little blind spot they really need to work on.

In the case of Japan, it’s easiest to understand if you think of it in terms of a household.
The Japanese government—the "husband"—borrows money from its citizens—the "wife"—to help cover household expenses.
In contrast, in countries like the United States or the United Kingdom, the "husbands" are so intimidated by their "wives" that they wouldn't dare ask them for a loan.
Instead, they keep borrowing money from other families.
Naturally, if you keep borrowing from other families, you have to expect them to raise the interest rates.
